newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: HIGHLIGHTS - Final WTO ministerial declaration.
newsitem.headline: HIGHLIGHTS - Final WTO ministerial declaration.

text.p: Ministers and officials from 128 countries adopted a wide-ranging final declaration at the end of the five-day World Trade Organisation (WTO) conference in Singapore on Friday.
The declaration said ministers "envisage a world where trade flows freely" and set out a programme to work to this end.
Following are the highlights of the declaration:
- Ministers said they believed the rapid change and increasing integration of the world economy offered "unprecedented opportunities for improved growth, job creation and development".
But they said this demanded adjustment by societies and posed challanges to the trading system.

- On the contentious labour issue, which has divided member states this week, the ministers declared they renewed their "commitment to the observance of internationally recognised core labour standards".
But they said the United Nations' International Labour Organisation (ILO) was the "competent body to set a deal on these standards", which could not be used for protectionist purposes.
- On service industries, the ministers pledged to achieve a successful conclusion of a pact on basic telecommunication by February 1997.
- Ministers welcomed the agreement initiated by the United States and the European Union to eliminate tariffs by the years 2000 on information technology products.
- The declaration committed ministers to "address the problem of marginalisation for the least developed countries" and the risk this posed for certain developing countries.

- Regional trade agreements were important, the ministers said, especially for developing and least developed countries. But they said the multilateral trading system managed by the WTO should take primacy.

- Without mentioning China or Russia -- the two biggest countries seeking membership of the WTO -- the ministers said the 28 countries applying to join the WTO should make "meaningful market access commitments".
They pledged their countries would work hard to bring the 28 into the WTO system quickly.
Integration of developing countries into the WTO system was "important for their economic development and for global trade expansion", the declaration said.

- Ministers said they were concerned by the problems of the least developed countries and had agreed to a plan of action "aimed at improving their overall capacity to respond to the opportunity offered by the trading system".
- After months of North-South battles, ministers also agreed to establish working groups in the WTO to look at the issues of trade and investment and trade and competition policy.
